Regulation VIII.-Reinstatement.
A person separated without delinquency or misconduct from an unclassified
iuev y position may be reinstated to a similar position tinder any department or inde-
pendent establishment, subject to the following limitations:
1J 3 (a) Unless otherwise provided hereinafter, an unclassified laborer may be
reinstated only upon certificate of the Commission and upon requisition
made within one year from the date of separation.
(b) A person honorably released from the active military or naval service of
the United States after service in the Civil War, War with Spain, or
War with Germany, or his widow, or an Army nurse of any wvar, may
be reinstated, if physically qualified, within five years from the date
of separation from his unclassified position; or, if a person served in
the \V with Germany, he may be reinstated within five years from
the date of his honorable discharge from the military or naval service.
(c) The widow of a veteran of the War with Germany formerly in the unclas-
sified service, who was the wife of such veteran while he was in the
military service, may be reinstated within five years from the date of
cessation of her husband's military service by death or otherwise
without discredit.
(d) A person separated from an unclassified position in the field service may
be reemployed in the same office within one year without certificate.
WARREN G HARDING

head:
]Executive erber.
Mr. Henry T. Ellington may be reinstated to the position of clerk in the
Railway Mail Service without regard to the length of his separation from the
service.
Mr. Ellington was removed from the position of clerk in the Railway Mail
Service on May 17, 1916, charged with embezzlement. The Postmaster General
states that he was tried and acquitted of the charge, that a most careful investi-
gation has convinced him that Mr. Ellington's removal was an injustice and
that he was entirely innocent of the charges made against him, and that his
reinstatement by executive order would serve the public interest better than
the appointment of a new clerk.
The Civil Service Commission concurs in recommending this order.
WARREN G HARDING
THE WHITE HOUSE,
May ,5, 1923.
[No. 3833.]

head:
Executive Order
Mr. Daniel R. Edwards may be appointed a contact representative in the
United States Veterans Bureau without examination under the civil service
rules. Mr. Edwards is a permanently disabled beneficiary of the Veterans
Bureau through the loss of an arm and a leg. He has been decorated with
the Distinguished Service Cross and twice with the Congressional Medal of
Honor.
The Director of the Veterans Bureau recommended Mr. Edwards' appoint-
ment, as he has been on trial and has given evidence that he can render good
service. The Director regards the case as exceptional, in that the appointment
would have a favorable psychological effect upon disabled ex-service men
because of Mr. Edwards' own disability and his clear conception of vocational
work, gained through his own training; and because of the association he has
had with welfare ex-service men's organizations.
The Civil Service Commission concurred in this recommendation.
WARREN G HARDING
THE WHITE HOUSE,
MUaY 22, 1923.
[No. 3854.]

head:

Mr. George L. Williams may be appointed to a position of laborer in the
Post Office Service without examination under the Civil Service Rules.
This order is issued on the recommendation of the Postmaster General
who states that while Mr. Williams was temporarily employed as mail mes-
senger at Jefferson City, Missouri, he was held up by bandits on March 1, 192 1,
who carried him into the country and bound him to a tree and escaped with
the registered pouches. He helped to identify the thieves when they were
arrested, and was many times threatened by their friends. He has been em-
ployed as a temporary laborer since June 1, 192 r.
Examinations have been held by the Civil Service Commission but no eli-
gibles have been obtained. Mr. Williams is 58 years of age and did not take
the examination as persons more than 45 years of age are not appointed in the
Postal Service.
The Civil Service Commission concurred in the recommendation.
WARREN G HARDING
THE WHITE HOUSE,
May 28, 1923.
[No. 3856.]

The Executive Order of February 14., 1912, as subsequently amended, per-
mitting employees in the executive civil service permanently residing in certain
incorporated municipalities adjacent to the District of Columbia to become
candidates for or hold municipal office therein, is hereby further amended so as
to include the incorporated municipality of Brentwood1, Maryland, among those
named in the order. The first paragraph of the order of l'ebruary 14, 1912, as
amended will read as follows:
Employees of the executive civil service permanently residing in the
following incorporated municipalities adjacent to the D istrict of Columbia
will not be prohibited from becoming candidates for or holding municipal
office in such corporations :
In Maryland-Takoma Park, Kensington, Garrett Park, Chevy Chase,
Glen Echo, Hyattsville, Mount Rainier, Somerset, North
Beach, Capitol Heights, Laurel, Riverdale, Bladensburg,
Brentwood.
& In Virginia-Fails Church, Vienna, Herndon, Potomac.
This order is recommended by the Civil Service Commission because it seems
necessary to the domestic interests of the Government employees, and for the
reason that similar conditions exist in Brentwood, Maryland, as in the other
municipalities named in the original order and its amendments. Brentwood is
almost surrounded by incorporated municipalities in which Government
employees have permission to participate in local political affairs.
